title: WebSockets & Real-Time Communication
summary: How a persistent full-duplex channel differs from request/response HTTP, how the upgrade handshake works, and when to reach for it versus SSE.

slides.sectionTitle: The limits of request/response for real-time
slides.markdown:
HTTP's model is client-asks, server-answers — the server can never speak first. That's a problem the moment you need the *server* to tell the client something unprompted: a new chat message, a live price tick, another player's move.

Forcing that need through request/response means the client has to keep asking "anything new?" over and over — workable, but wasteful and laggy compared to the server just saying so the moment it happens.

| | Polling | Long polling | WebSockets |
|---|---|---|
| Pattern | Client asks every N seconds | Client asks, server holds the request open until there's news | Client and server both send anytime, over one open connection |
| Latency | Up to N seconds | Near-instant, but re-opens per update | Instant, no reopening |
| Overhead | New request every interval | New request per update | One handshake, then just frames |

Each step is solving the previous one's core problem: polling wastes requests, long polling still re-opens per message, WebSockets finally removes both costs.

A WebSocket connection starts as a normal HTTP request with one special header: `Upgrade: websocket`. If the server agrees, it replies `101 Switching Protocols` — from that moment, the *same* TCP connection stops speaking HTTP and starts speaking WebSocket framing.

![HTTP request upgrading into a persistent WebSocket connection](assets/websocket-upgrade.svg)

This is why WebSockets pass through existing HTTP infrastructure almost for free — it starts as a request they already understand. See [HTTP Fundamentals](http-fundamentals).

assets.alt: HTTP request upgrading into a persistent WebSocket connection

slides.markdown:
Once upgraded, both sides can send **frames** to each other at any time, in either direction, independently — no more strict "client asks, server answers" turn-taking. A frame can carry text, binary data, or a control signal (ping/pong, close).

This is the actual feature that makes WebSockets different from long polling: it's not just faster, it's a fundamentally different communication shape — bidirectional and unprompted, not request-driven.

A WebSocket connection can sit idle for a long time with no application data flowing — which looks identical, from the network's perspective, to a dead connection. **Ping/pong control frames** solve this: one side pings periodically, the other must pong back, or the connection is assumed dead and closed.

This matters operationally because idle connections without heartbeat traffic often get silently killed by NAT gateways or load balancers after a timeout, well before either endpoint notices anything is wrong.

A WebSocket connection is *stateful and long-lived*, unlike a stateless HTTP request — that breaks the usual scaling playbook. A client's connection is pinned to whichever server instance handled the handshake, so "sticky sessions" become necessary, not optional.

Broadcasting to all connected clients then needs a shared pub/sub layer (Redis, Kafka) fanning messages out across instances, or clients on different instances simply can't reach each other. See [Load Balancing](load-balancing-layers-algorithms).

slides.sectionTitle: Server-Sent Events as a simpler alternative
slides.markdown:
| | WebSockets | Server-Sent Events (SSE) |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Bidirectional | Server-to-client only |
| Protocol | Custom framing after upgrade | Plain HTTP, just a long-lived response stream |
| Complexity | Higher — custom client/server handling | Lower — built on standard HTTP, auto-reconnect built into browsers |

How to decide: if the client only ever *receives* updates (live scores, notifications, a stock ticker) and never needs to push data back over the same channel, SSE is simpler and gets you there with less machinery.

slides.sectionTitle: The upgrade into a persistent channel
slides.markdown:
One picture worth internalizing: an ordinary HTTP request/response pair (with the `Upgrade` header) transforms in place into an open, bidirectional, persistent connection — no new TCP connection, no new port, just a protocol switch on the existing one.

![HTTP handshake transitioning into a persistent bidirectional WebSocket connection](assets/websocket-persistent-channel.svg)

Everything after that point is WebSocket frames, not HTTP requests, until either side sends a close frame.

assets.alt: HTTP handshake transitioning into a persistent bidirectional WebSocket connection

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reaching for WebSockets by default
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Real-time feature = WebSockets, always."

**Why it's wrong:** WebSockets bring real cost — stateful connections, sticky sessions, reconnect logic, a pub/sub layer to fan out messages. If updates only flow one way, that's a lot of machinery for something SSE or polling could handle more simply.

**Correct model:** match the tool to the requirement's shape. Bidirectional, high-frequency, low-latency traffic (chat, gaming, collaborative editing) genuinely needs WebSockets; a dashboard refreshing every few seconds usually doesn't.
